questions.question: A certain processor uses a fully associative cache of size 16 kB, The cache block size is 16 bytes. Assume that the main memory is byte addressable and uses a 32-bit address. How many bits are required for the Tag and the Index fields respectively in the addresses generated by the processor?
questions.explanation:
Fully associative cache has no index field (a block can go in any line).

Block size 16 bytes [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] offset = 4 bits. Tag = 32 [latex]-[/latex] 4 = 28 bits.

Answer: 28 bits and 0 bits

questions.question:
Let [latex]U=\{1,2,,...n\}[/latex]. Let [latex]A=\{(x,X)|x\in X,X\subseteq U\}[/latex]. Consider the following two statements on |A|.

I. [latex]|A|=n2^{n-1}[/latex]
II. [latex]|A|=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\binom{n}{k}[/latex]

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Count the pairs (x, X) with [latex]x\in X[/latex] in two ways:
- Fix x first: x lies in [latex]2^{n-1}[/latex] subsets, so [latex]|A|=n\,2^{n-1}[/latex].
- Fix the size k of X first: there are [latex]\binom nk[/latex] such sets, each giving k choices of x, so [latex]|A|=\sum_{k=1}^{n}k\binom nk[/latex].

Both are correct (and equal).

Answer: Both I and II

- If xy = 0, x and y are never both 1, so XOR equals OR [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.
- [latex]xy+x'y'[/latex] is XNOR; its complement is XOR [latex]\text{---}[/latex] valid.

questions.question:
Let X be a square matrix. Consider the following two statements on X.

I. X is invertible
II. Determinant of X is non-zero

Which one of the following is TRUE?

options.A: I implies II; II does not imply I
options.B: II implies I; I does not imply II
options.C: I does not imply II; II does not imply I
options.D: I and II are equivalent statements

questions.explanation:
A square matrix is invertible if and only if its determinant is non-zero ([latex]X^{-1}=\frac{adj(X)}{\det X}[/latex]). So I and II imply each other.

Answer: I and II are equivalent statements

questions.question:
Let G be an arbitrary group. Consider the following relations on G:

R1: [latex]\forall a,b \in G, aR_1b[/latex] if and only if [latex]\exists g \in G[/latex] such that [latex]a=g^{-1}bg[/latex]
R2: [latex]\forall a,b \in G, aR_2b[/latex] if and only if [latex]a=b^{-1}[/latex]

Which of the above is/are equivalence relation/relations?
questions.explanation:
R1 (conjugacy):
- Reflexive: [latex]a=e^{-1}ae[/latex]
- Symmetric: if [latex]a=g^{-1}bg[/latex] then [latex]b=gag^{-1}[/latex]
- Transitive: [latex]a=g^{-1}bg,\ b=h^{-1}ch\Rightarrow a=(hg)^{-1}c(hg)[/latex]
So R1 is an equivalence relation.

R2: aR2a would need [latex]a=a^{-1}[/latex], which fails in general (e.g. 1 in [latex]\mathbb{Z}_3[/latex]). Not reflexive.

Answer: R1 only

questions.question:
Consider the following two statements about database transaction schedules:

I. Strict two-phase locking protocol generates conflict serializable schedules that are also recoverable.
II. Timestamp-ordering concurrency control protocol with Thomas' Write Rule can generate view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable.

Which of the above statements is/are TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Strict 2PL holds all exclusive locks until commit, so schedules are conflict serializable and no transaction reads uncommitted data [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] recoverable [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- Thomas' write rule ignores obsolete writes, which allows some view serializable schedules that are not conflict serializable (blind writes) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.

Answer: Both I and II

questions.question:
Consider three concurrent processes P1, P2 and P3 as shown below, which access a shared variable D that has been initialized to 100.

The process are executed on a uniprocessor system running a time-shared operating system. If the minimum and maximum possible values of D after the three processes have completed execution are X and Y respectively, then the value of Y-X is __________.
questions.explanation:
Each update is really load D, change, store D, so a process can overwrite the others' results.

- Maximum: lose P2's update. P1 reads 100; P2 runs fully (D = 50); P1 writes 120; then P3 makes it 130. So [latex]Y=130[/latex].
- Minimum: lose both additions. P2 reads 100; P1 and P3 run fully (D = 130); P2 writes 100 [latex]-[/latex] 50 = 50. So [latex]X=50[/latex].

[latex]Y-X=130-50=80[/latex]

Answer: 80

Answer: 29

questions.question: Consider three machines M, N and P with IP addresses 100.10.5.2, 100.10.5.5 and 100.10.5.6 respectively. The subnet mask is set to 255.255.255.252 for all the three machines. Which one of the following is true?

options.A: M, N and P all belong to the same subnet
options.B: Only M and N belong to the same subnet
options.C: Only N and P belong to the same subnet
options.D: M, N, and P belong to three different subnets

Mask 255.255.255.252 = /30, so subnets are blocks of 4 in the last octet.
- M: .2 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block .0-.3
- N: .5 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block .4-.7
- P: .6 [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] block .4-.7

questions.question: Suppose that in an IP-over-Ethernet network, a machine X wishes to find the MAC address of another machine Y in its subnet. Which one of the following techniques can be used for this?

options.A: X sends an ARP request packet to the local gateway's IP address which then finds the  MAC address of Y and sends to X
options.B: X sends an ARP request packet to the local gateway's MAC address which then finds the MAC address of Y and sends to X
options.C: X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast MAC address in its local subnet
options.D: X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast IP address in its local subnet

questions.explanation:
ARP request: X does not know Y's MAC, so it sends the request to the broadcast MAC address (FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF) in its subnet, carrying Y's IP. Only Y replies, with its MAC.

The gateway is not involved (Y is in the same subnet), and ARP does not use a broadcast IP address.

Answer: X sends an ARP request packet with broadcast MAC address in its local subnet

questions.question:
Consider three 4-variable functions [latex]f_1,f_2 \; and \; f_3[/latex], which are expressed in sum-of-minterms

[latex]f_1=\Sigma (0,2,5,8,14)[/latex]
[latex]f_2=\Sigma (2,3,6,8,14,15)[/latex]
[latex]f_3=\Sigma (2,7,11,14)[/latex]

For the following circuit with one AND gate and one XOR gate, the output function f can be expressed as:

Circuit: [latex]f=(f_1\cdot f_2)\oplus f_3[/latex].

- [latex]f_1\cdot f_2[/latex] = common minterms = {2, 8, 14}
- XOR with [latex]f_3[/latex] = {2, 7, 11, 14}: keep minterms in exactly one set [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] 2 and 14 cancel, leaving {7, 8, 11}

Answer: [latex]\Sigma(7,8,11)[/latex]

questions.question: Which one of the following languages over [latex]\Sigma =\{a,b\}[/latex] is NOT context-free?

Checking each statement:

- [latex]wa^nb^nw^R[/latex]: nested matching (w with [latex]w^R[/latex] outside, a's with b's inside) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] CFL.
- [latex]\{a^nb^i\mid i\in\{n,3n,5n\}\}[/latex]: union of three CFLs [latex]\text{---}[/latex] CFL.
- [latex]wa^nw^Rb^n[/latex]: the w-[latex]w^R[/latex] match and the a-b match cross each other, which one stack cannot handle [latex]\text{---}[/latex] not CFL.

questions.question:
Let the set of functional dependencies [latex]F=\{QR\rightarrow S,R\rightarrow P,S\rightarrow Q\}[/latex] hold on a relation schema X = (PQRS). X is not in BCNF. Suppose X is decomposed into two schemas Y and Z where Y = (PR) and Z = (QRS).
Consider the two statements given below:

I. Both Y and Z are in BCNF
II. Decomposition of X into Y and Z is dependency preserving and lossless.

Which of the above statements is/are correct?
questions.explanation:
Checking each statement:
- Y(P, R): R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P with R as key [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] BCNF.
- Z(Q, R, S): QR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S and S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q. Keys are QR and RS. In S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q, S is not a superkey [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Z is not BCNF. So I is false.
- Dependencies: R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P is in Y; QR [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] S and S [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] Q are in Z [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] preserved.
- Lossless: common attribute R, and R [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] P makes R a key of Y [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] lossless. So II is true.

Answer: II only

questions.question: Assume that in a certain computer, the virtual addresses are 64 bits long and the physical addresses are 48 bits long. The memory is word addressable. The page size is 8kB and the word size is 4 bytes. The Translation Look-aside Buffer (TLB) in the address translation path has 128 valid entries. At most how many distinct virtual addresses can be translated without any TLB miss?
questions.explanation:
Word addressable, word = 4 bytes, so one page = 8 KB / 4 B = [latex]2^{11}[/latex] words = 2048 addresses.

128 TLB entries cover 128 pages: [latex]128\times2^{11}=2^{18}=256\times2^{10}[/latex] addresses without a TLB miss.

Answer: [latex]256\times2^{10}[/latex]

questions.question:
Consider the following sets:

S1: Set of all recursively enumerable languages over the alphabet {0, 1}.
S2: Set of all syntactically valid C programs.
S3: Set of all languages over the alphabet {0, 1}.
S4: Set of all non-regular languages over the alphabet {0, 1}.

Which of the above sets are uncountable?

Checking each statement:
- S1: every RE language has a TM, and TMs can be listed [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] countable.
- S2: C programs are finite strings [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] countable.
- S3: all languages = the power set of [latex]\{0,1\}^*[/latex] [latex]\rightarrow[/latex] uncountable.
- S4: S3 minus the countably many regular languages is still uncountable.

Answer: S3 and S4

Consider the first order predicate formula:
[latex]\forall x[\forall z\; z|x\Rightarrow ((z=x)\vee (z=1))\Rightarrow[/latex] [latex]\exists w(w> x)\wedge (\forall z \; z|w\Rightarrow ((w=z)\vee (z=1)))][/latex]

questions.question: There are n unsorted arrays: [latex]A_1,A_2,...,A_n[/latex]. Assume that n is odd. Each of [latex]A_1,A_2,...,A_n[/latex] contains n distinct elements. There are no common elements between any two arrays. The worst-case Asymptotic Notation of computing the median of the medians of [latex]A_1,A_2,...,A_n[/latex] is ________ .

questions.question:
Let G be any connection, weighted, undirected graph:

I. G has a unique minimum spanning tree if no two edges of G have the same weight.
II. G has a unique minimum spanning tree if, for every cut of G, there is a unique minimum weight edge crossing the cut.

Which of the above two statements is/are TRUE?

questions.question: Consider the following snapshot of a system running n concurrent processes. Process [latex]i[/latex] is holding [latex]X_i[/latex] instances of a resource R, [latex] 1\leq i\leq n[/latex]. Assume that all instances of R are currently in use. Further, for all [latex]i[/latex], process [latex]i[/latex] can place a request for at most [latex]Y_i[/latex] additional instances of R while holding the [latex]X_i[/latex] instances it already has. Of the n processes, there are exactly two processes p and q such that [latex]Y_p=Y_q=0[/latex]. questions.question: A certain processor deploys a single-level cache. The cache block size is 8 words and the word size is 4 bytes. The memory system uses a 60-MHz clock. To service a cache-miss, the memory controller first takes 1 cycle to accept the starting address of the block, it then takes 3 cycles to fetch all the eight words of the block, and finally transmits the words of the requested block at the rate of 1 word per cycle. The maximum bandwidth for the memory system when the program running on the processor issues a series of read operations is _________[latex]\times 10^6[/latex] bytes/sec.
questions.explanation:
One cache miss brings one block of 8 words [latex]\times[/latex] 4 bytes = 32 bytes.
Cycles per block = 1 (address) + 3 (fetch) + 8 (transfer, 1 word per cycle) = 12 cycles.

Time per block = 12 / 60 MHz = 0.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s.
Bandwidth = 32 bytes / 0.2 [latex]\mu[/latex]s = [latex]160\times10^6[/latex] bytes/s

Answer: 160
